stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: For three winters, astronomer Leila Okafor recorded the brightness of a faint red dwarf in the constellation Lynx, taking a measurement every four minutes. The resulting light curve was mostly flat, and for days at a stretch the star's output barely ______ without warning about once a week, the star would double its brightness for several minutes before fading back to its usual glow. Such flares, Okafor argues, could gradually strip the atmosphere from any planet orbiting close by.
explanation: Cover the blank and test each side. "The resulting light curve was mostly flat, and for days at a stretch the star's output barely changed" can stand alone as a sentence. What comes after looks like a modifier because it starts with "flaring," but keep reading: "the star would double its brightness" has its own subject and verb. That makes "flaring without warning about once a week, the star would double its brightness..." a complete sentence too. Two complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon, so "changed; flaring" is correct.

A.why: You took "flaring..." for a modifier attached to the first clause and stopped reading before "the star would double." That later subject and verb make the second part a complete sentence, so a comma alone between the two creates a comma splice.

C.why: You let the two complete sentences run together with no punctuation at all. This fuses "the star's output barely changed" directly into a second independent clause, which makes a run-on.

D.why: You chose the comma-plus-conjunction pattern, which is a legal way to join two sentences, but "so" signals cause and effect. The star staying steady most of the time does not cause it to flare. The two ideas contrast, so "so" gives the sentence the wrong logic.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When the coastal county of Aldenport began mailing free radon test kits to rural households in 2018, public health officials expected that only a small share would ever be returned. Many residents, after all, had ignored earlier mailings about well-water safety. The response to the kits surprised the officials______ more than 60 percent of the kits came back within two months, and dozens arrived with handwritten notes asking how to arrange follow-up testing.
explanation: Cover the blank and test each side. "The response to the kits surprised the officials" is a complete sentence. "More than 60 percent of the kits came back within two months..." is also a complete sentence. Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, a colon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word. The first sentence also points forward: it says the officials were surprised, and the second sentence explains what surprised them. A colon is the mark that delivers that explanation, so it is the correct choice.

A.why: You chose a comma splice. The pause before the explanation sounds natural, but a comma by itself can't join two complete sentences.

B.why: You let two complete sentences run together with no punctuation at all, which makes a fused sentence.

D.why: You joined two complete sentences with "and" but no comma before it. The second sentence also already contains its own "and," so the result reads as a run-on.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Over three winters in the early 1990s, folklorist Ines Varga traveled by ferry between fishing villages in the Danube Delta, recording elderly residents as they told stories about river spirits, drowned bells, and enchanted sturgeon. She often stayed with one family for weeks so that she could hear each tale told more than once______ transcribed and annotated by her graduate students, those recordings now form the largest archive of the region's fishing legends.
explanation: Cover the blank. "She often stayed with one family for weeks so that she could hear each tale told more than once" is a complete sentence. After the blank, the participle phrase "transcribed and annotated by her graduate students" leads into a subject and verb, "those recordings now form," so that side is a complete sentence too. Two complete sentences need strong punctuation between them, and a period supplies it.

A.why: You fell for the leading participle. "Transcribed" made the second half look like a modifier, but "those recordings now form" makes it a full sentence, so the comma creates a comma splice.

B.why: You put no punctuation between two complete sentences. This also makes "transcribed" seem to describe "once," which makes no sense.

C.why: You joined two complete sentences with "and" and no comma. Because the second sentence opens with its own participle phrase, the result is an ungrammatical run-on.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The dozens of clay-lined storage pits on the hillside at Tell Karsa were all built in the same shape and to roughly the same depth. For years, excavators took this uniformity as evidence that the pits had been dug by a single community over a short period______ radiocarbon dates from the charred barley found inside them span nearly four centuries, which suggests a building tradition passed down across many generations.
explanation: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences. "Excavators took this uniformity as evidence..." can stand alone, and so can "radiocarbon dates... span nearly four centuries." The contrast word "however" belongs to the second sentence, because that sentence is the one that overturns the assumption. The semicolon should therefore go before "however," with a comma after it.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. A word like "however" is not a FANBOYS conjunction, so commas around it can't join two complete sentences.

C.why: You placed the semicolon after "however," which attaches the contrast to the excavators' assumption. The contrast actually comes from the new radiocarbon dates in the second sentence.

D.why: You left nothing before "however" and only a comma after it. That puts no legal boundary between the two complete sentences, so the result is a comma splice.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Nutrition researchers studying bone health in older adults paid special attention to vitamin K2, a nutrient that helps the body direct calcium into the skeleton. Fermented soybean foods such as natto contain some of the highest concentrations of K2 found in any food______ most participants in the study's sample said they rarely or never ate these foods, so their measured intake of the vitamin remained low.
explanation: Each side of the blank is a complete sentence, so you need a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word. The two ideas contrast: natto is rich in K2, yet participants rarely ate it. A comma followed by "but" joins the sentences correctly and also signals that contrast.

A.why: The punctuation is legal, but "so" signals cause and effect. Natto being rich in K2 is not the reason participants avoided it, so the logic is wrong.

C.why: You chose a comma splice. The comma sounds like a natural pause, but on its own it can't join two complete sentences.

D.why: You chose the right conjunction but left out the comma that must come before "but" when it joins two complete sentences.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Self-healing concrete contains dormant bacteria that wake up when water seeps into a crack. To test a new formulation, engineers at a materials laboratory in Trondheim, Norway, deliberately cracked a set of sample beams and then submerged them in water______ within three weeks, the bacteria embedded in the mix had produced enough limestone to seal gaps up to 0.8 millimeters wide.
explanation: "Engineers... deliberately cracked a set of sample beams and then submerged them in water" is a complete sentence. "Within three weeks, the bacteria... had produced enough limestone..." is also complete, with "bacteria" as its subject and "had produced" as its verb. A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why: You chose a comma splice. The introductory phrase "within three weeks" makes the second half look like a continuation, but it has its own subject and verb, so a comma alone can't join it.

C.why: You ran two complete sentences together with no punctuation. This also makes "within three weeks" seem to describe how long the beams were submerged.

D.why: You used the FANBOYS word "so" without the comma that must come before it, which leaves two complete sentences fused together.
